statements.quote: The three math chapters before this one gave you the *numbers* a neural network manipulates — sums, products, vectors, gradients.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: This chapter gives you the *stage* on which those numbers live: **space**, and the history of how we came to understand it.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: Geometry is older than almost any other branch of mathematics.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: Arithmetic needs counting; geometry needs a *landscape* to measure, a field to bound, a temple to square.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: It is also, arguably, the most visual and the most "alive" of the disciplines — and the quote above, written for a modern textbook on the *shape of space* \citeauthor{weeksshapespace} (\citeyear{weeksshapespace}), makes the point: geometry is not a relic finished off in Alexandria.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: Every few centuries it has had to grow, because real surfaces and models no longer fit inside flat, straight-line space.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: This chapter follows that growth step by step.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: For each turn we ask four questions: **what** was discovered, **who** did it, **when**, and — the question that makes a history interesting — **why**, what need of the age forced the result to exist.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: We start where the physical evidence actually begins: with a hand tool pressing a zig-zag into a river shell, long before any Greek theorist.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: We then cross the first cities, where geometry became a *job* (surveying land after the flood), pass through the Greek invention of *proof*, the medieval and early-modern reformulation of space in terms of projection and coordinates, and finally the 19th-century discovery that space need not be *flat* — the idea that later made general relativity possible, and that underlies the high-dimensional "spaces of meaning" you will meet in the [Embeddings](embeddinglab) chapter.
statements.section: Why geometry

statements.quote: The oldest geometric objects we have are marks and shapes rather than calculations.

statements.quote: For most of its early history geometry was not a body of theorems but a *technique of state*: the discipline of measuring fields, dividing inheritances, and erecting temples that had to be square — and it appears almost simultaneously in the first great urban cultures (Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, China), each with its own tools and its own number system.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: The reason was a single, shared, unglamorous fact of land: **when the river rose, the boundaries vanished.**
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: In Egypt the Nile's annual inundation wiped out every field boundary, and each year the fields had to be *re-measured* — and, crucially, the crown's grain tax was assessed by the *area* of a holding, so a wrong area meant a wrong tax.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: In Mesopotamia, where there was no single river but a dense mesh of canals and private plots, the need to settle *disputable* boundaries between neighbours was constant.
statements.section: II. Measuring the land: the surveyor's equations

statements.quote: In China the state had to tax land, move armies, and move earth (dikes, canals, granaries), and every one of those is a *geometry* problem.

statements.quote: A **scheme** is a space whose "points" are not locations but *solutions of polynomial equations*; a **topos** is a space so general that it may have no points at all — it is recorded by the sheaves of functions that can be planted in it, and the space itself is defined *by those functions* \cite{grothedieck_ega1960}.

statements.quote: The consequences sound like pure philosophy and are pure mathematics.
